items.stem: A returns-processing agent holds five role-scoped tools used in one refund decision: lookup, return-window check, fraud flag, refund issuance, and credit application. Ahead of peak volume, a reviewer proposes splitting it into eligibility and execution agents for Finance. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Split into eligibility and execution agents, adding a shared correlation ID so both calls trace to one refund request.
Split into a role-scoped eligibility agent and a role-scoped execution agent, as the reviewer proposes.
Remove the fraud-flag tool so the agent holds four tools instead of five, avoiding the need to split at all.
Keep the tools in one agent; splitting would separate return-window check from refund issuance, risking stale eligibility.

items.whyRight: The five tools already form a small, single-role decision set — exactly the range scoping is meant to produce, not the oversized, multi-role sprawl the split remedy targets. Splitting a set this size doesn't shrink any decision space; it only adds an unneeded coordination hop between agents.

whyWrong.A: A shared correlation ID makes the split traceable, but traceability doesn't answer whether splitting was needed — it wasn't, since five tools were never an oversized decision space.
whyWrong.B: This is the answer for an oversized, multi-role tool surface; splitting a genuinely small, single-decision set of five tools adds a hop this scenario never needed.
whyWrong.C: Fraud review is a needed capability the workflow uses, not the cause of the split proposal; removing it sidesteps the question instead of answering it.

items.t1Clause: the agent already holds only five role-scoped tools used together in one refund decision
items.lessonKey: agent check eligibility issuance keep one refund return risking separate splitting stale tools window would

items.stem: A weekly invoice-reconciliation job processes 80,000 line items against a 2-hour runtime budget and keeps exceeding it. It waits for each complete model response before validating and posting to the ledger; an engineer proposes streaming to close the gap. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Enable streaming and report the improved time-to-first-token against the 2-hour runtime budget.
Reject streaming for this consumer and reduce total latency at the pipeline's slowest measured stage.
Enable streaming and report the run's improved mean per-item response time, while total weekly runtime still exceeds the 2-hour budget.
Add a monitoring alert that flags runtime-budget breaches after each weekly run, leaving the pipeline itself unchanged.

items.whyRight: The pipeline waits for each complete response before writing downstream, so time-to-first-token never mattered here; total latency is unchanged by streaming, and the SLA breach can only close by reducing time at the slowest measured stage.

whyWrong.A: Time-to-first-token only matters to a consumer reading incrementally; this pipeline waits for the complete response, so the reported metric never touches the 2-hour runtime budget it actually misses.
whyWrong.C: A mean per-item improvement can still leave the weekly run's total processing time over its 2-hour budget; streaming buys nothing for a consumer waiting on the full response before posting.
whyWrong.D: Flagging breaches after each weekly run confirms the budget was missed again; it does nothing to shorten the pipeline's slowest stage, which is what the miss is caused by.

items.t1Clause: parses each complete model response before writing downstream
